title: Letters to Four Struggling Churches
overview: The risen Jesus sends frank messages to four churches in what is now western Turkey, praising their strengths, naming their faults, and promising rewards to those who stay faithful.

parts.label: Ephesus praised (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Each letter is addressed to a church's 'angel,' which may mean its leader or a heavenly guardian; scholars are unsure. Ephesus is praised for tireless work, patient endurance, and for testing people who claimed to be apostles and finding them false.

parts.label: Ephesus warned (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: Yet the church has lost the love it had at first, and unless it turns back, its lamp, meaning its life as a church, will be removed. It is credited for rejecting the Nicolaitans, a group no one can identify for certain (possibly the same teaching described in vv. 14-15), and the faithful are promised the tree of life, closed off since Eden.

parts.label: Smyrna: poor yet rich (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: This poor, persecuted church is warned that some will be jailed, but the trial is limited ('ten days' likely means a short time), and those faithful even to death are promised a life that the second death, final judgment, cannot harm. The harsh phrase 'synagogue of Satan' comes from a bitter local dispute over who truly belonged to God's people; most scholars stress it is no verdict on Jewish people, though it has been tragically misused that way.

parts.label: Pergamum: loyal but compromised (vv. 12-17)
parts.note: Pergamum, perhaps called the place of Satan's throne because of its temples and emperor worship, stayed loyal even when a believer named Antipas was killed, but some members followed the way of Balaam, who in the book of Numbers led Israel into idol feasts and sexual sin. Instead of idol meals, the faithful are promised hidden manna, the desert bread God once gave, and a white stone with a secret new name, whose meaning is uncertain (perhaps a token of acquittal, a ticket to a feast, or a sign of new identity).

parts.label: Thyatira and 'Jezebel' (vv. 18-23)
parts.note: Thyatira is growing in love and service but tolerates a self-proclaimed prophet nicknamed Jezebel, after the queen who drew Israel to idols, whose teaching allowed food offered to idols and sexual sin; whether that is literal or, as often in the prophets, a picture of unfaithfulness to God is debated. After she refuses time to change, the threats are stark: a bed, most likely of sickness (some translations spell this out), for her and her partners, and death for her children, probably meaning her followers.

parts.label: A light load for the faithful (vv. 24-29)
parts.note: Those who rejected her teaching, which boasted of deep knowledge the text ties to Satan (it is unclear whether that was her group's own phrase or a mocking label), are asked only to hold on. Their reward borrows the harsh image from Psalm 2 of smashing nations like pottery to share Jesus' authority with them, along with the morning star, which the book later names as Jesus himself (22:16).

disagreement: Most Christians read these as letters to real first-century churches that also speak to churches everywhere, while some, especially in certain Protestant traditions, also see the churches as a preview of successive ages of church history.
think: Can a person keep doing the right things for years after the love that started them has faded, and what would that look like from the inside?
